newsitem.title: USA: U.S. base metal premiums steady, copper scrap busy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. base metal premiums steady, copper scrap busy.

text.p: Base metal premiums in the United States were largely unchanged from last week, with some delays to aluminum shipments from the Northwest to the Midwest not yet causing upward price pressure, traders said.
Aluminum premiums were quoted at 5.50 to 6.00 cents per pound over LME cash on metal for prompt delivery, falling to below 5.00 cents for the second half of the year.
Some dealers noted that flooding in the Northern plains in the Dakotas have caused some delays in shipments from smelters in the Pacific Northwest to the Midwest.

"We are seeing delays of about two weeks due to problems with some rail lines and trucks not able to get through," one dealer said. There appeared to be enough metal available for consumers and a spike in premiums was unlikely, the dealer added.
Zinc and nickel dealers were awaiting the outcome of this week's U.S. Mint tenders to see if premiums shift.
Tenders for 2,499 tonnes of special high grade zinc were due in Thursday morning, while offers to sell 220 tonnes of nickel were due in Wednesday afternoon.

Zinc premiums were unchanged at 5.25 to 5.75 cents per pound over LME cash with spot physical business quiet. Some dealers noted that due to higher LME zinc prices, dealers may be tempted to offer metal to the Mint at lower premiums.
Both tin and nickel physical markets were stable with only modest activity.
The copper scrap market sprung into life this week as merchants eagerly lined up to sell and make the most of the surge in red metal prices.
"It's hopping," according to an East coast dealer.

Aluminum scrap is still fairly tight and prices firm, but the A380 grade aluminum alloy prices remained lackluster, quoted at 73.5 to 75.00 cents per pound, delivered Midwest, down from 76-77 cents earlier this month, and putting more pressure on already "non-existent" smelter margins, an alloy seller said.
